[RAZI-FULL:v7p121/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | If God speaks the clause, it answers the believers' plea for forgiveness: after their obedience and request for pardon over deliberate shortcomings, He reassures them about inadvertent lapses. | mentions 2:285
[RAZI-FULL:v7p121/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The verb is used in the construction “I burdened him with a thing, so he undertook it”; taklīf is its verbal noun.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p121/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ treats wusʿ as a noun, like wajd and juhd.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p121/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعضهم | reports | Others define capacity as what a person can bear without constriction or hardship, below the utmost degree of exertion.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p122/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The second argument says acts depend on motives created by God; if motives instead came from the person, an infinite regress follows, while a determining motive makes the alternative impossible, yet the unbeliever is commanded to believe.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p122/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The third argument says a command issued when motives are equal requires contradictory equality and preference; if one motive prevails, the preferred is necessary and the other impossible.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p122/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The fourth argument says Abū Lahab was commanded to believe even though God had announced that he would not believe, so he was required to believe that he would not believe.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p122/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The fifth argument says people do not know the detailed count of movements and rests in an act such as moving a finger; since they did not intend that precise count, they do not create it, and an undetermined preference is impossible.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p122/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | Al-Rāzī deems the rational proofs decisive: when they conflict with an apparent scriptural meaning, one must preserve the proofs and interpret the apparent text, or undermine rational grounds for monotheism, prophecy, and scripture.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p122/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-Rāzī notes that the same interpretive method is routinely used by the Muʿtazila against anthropomorphic readings; thus the verse certainly admits interpretation even if its precise interpretation is left unspecified.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p123/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A second answer defines command as notice that action brings reward and omission brings punishment; where an act is impossible, the statement is not a real command but notice of punishment and one's creation for Hell.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p123/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · طائفة من قدماء أهل الجبر | reports | A group of early determinists says people are commanded while it remains unknown whether God knows they will die unbelievers; after such a death, one learns the obstacle was present and the condition for obligation had been absent during life.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p123/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | A fourth answer says the clause is spoken by the believers and therefore does not prove God's rule; al-Rāzī calls this weak, since God recounts and praises their words, so they must be truthful.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p761/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the verb is repeated in different forms simply to vary the style, as in the pairing of مهل and أمهل. | mentions 77:11
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p761/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Abū Ḥayyān instead says good deeds are acquired without strain by following God's command, while sins require effort to cross the boundary of His prohibition, explaining the two verb forms.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p762/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · السجاوندي | reports | Al-Sajāwandī explains the intensified form by saying evil clings to its doer, while good may be shared through guidance and intercession; iftiʿāl also suggests contraction, as the soul contracts into evil.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p762/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · عطاء | reports | ʿAṭāʾ glosses “we forgot” as “we did not know” and “we erred” as “we acted deliberately.”
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p762/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قطرب، والطبري | reports | Quṭrub and al-Ṭabarī gloss نسينا as “we left/omitted”; the source then begins their gloss of وأخطأنا.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p762/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Good is framed as belonging to the soul, while evil is placed over it as a weight it bears, like having wealth but owing a debt.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p762/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The supplication is implicitly introduced by “say”; prayer is the core of worship because the petitioner sees personal need and abasement and God's self-sufficiency and generosity, fittingly closing the sūra.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p762/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Each petition begins Rabbana to invoke God as their nurturer and reformer and to acknowledge their servitude and need; final clauses omit it because they conclude earlier petitions.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p762/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The final three pleas answer the first three: pardon answers “do not hold us accountable,” forgiveness answers “do not lay a burden,” and mercy answers “do not impose what we cannot bear.”
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p762/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The basic meaning of مؤاخذة is consequence or requital; here fāʿala may simply mean the basic verb أخذ. | mentions 29:40
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p762/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another explanation retains the reciprocal form because the sinner makes himself vulnerable to punishment through his deed, as though aiding his own injury.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p762/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | A further explanation says God takes the sinner in punishment while the sinner appeals to God for pardon and generosity, so each is figuratively described as taking the other.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p762/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Forgetting is absence of recollection, and forgetfulness and error are excused from accountability.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p763/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الطبري | reports | Al-Tabari glosses the wording about error as “we intended,” while Qutrub says it means we missed the correct interpretation.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p763/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الأصمعي | reports | Al-Asmai distinguishes أخطأ as an unintended mistake from خطئ as deliberate wrongdoing; the cited poem witnesses the latter.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p763/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Zamakhshari permits taking forgetting and error literally as excused lapses, and also reads them as negligence and inattention that caused the lapse; God’s faithful servants seek continued protection from such lapses. | mentions 18:63
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p763/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عطية | prefers | Ibn Atiyya says many scholars correctly understand the prayer as asking pardon for prevailing forgetfulness and error from the intended course.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p763/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قتادة | reports | Qatada reports that the Prophet said God has pardoned his community for forgetfulness and error.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p763/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddi says the believers feared accountability when the verse came, then Gabriel told the Prophet that God had granted their request.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p763/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | These reports support asking relief from involuntary forgetfulness and error after the believers feared the prior verse’s reckoning. | mentions 2:284
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p763/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Some lapses are culpable when a person neglects precautions, such as forgetting known impurity in clothing after failing to take steps to remember.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p763/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another view makes the prayer hypothetical: even if forgetfulness could warrant accountability, pardon is requested because constant vigilance would be burdensome.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Some infer from this verse that God may impose a duty beyond human capacity.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قتادة | reports | A report from Qatada interprets isr as the hastening of punishment.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj takes isr as a trial that tests people, like killing and wounding among the Israelites or making a silver ceiling for a disbeliever.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari derives isr from a burden that holds its bearer in place, metaphorically describing harsh duties such as self-killing and cutting impurity from skin or clothing.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r13] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · القفال | reports | Al-Qaffal says readers of the fifth book of the Torah attributed to the Jews will find many remarkable instances of their grave covenants and pledges.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r14] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبي | reports | Ubayy reads the verb with gemination and uses the plural form asara.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r15] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · عاصم | reports | A reading reported from Asim has the hamza of isr with a damma.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r16] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The people before the believers here are the Jews.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r17] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Dahhak says the people before them include Christians as well.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r18] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قتادة | reports | Qatada reads the prayer as asking God not to impose the severity imposed on earlier people.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r19] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Dahhak, with Ibn Zayd, interprets the prayer as asking not to be burdened with deeds beyond one's capacity.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | One view finds here forgiveness for major sinners: the prayer would be improper if forgetfulness and error meant only unaccountable acts, so they signify deliberate sin, omission and commission respectively.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r20] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن جريج | reports | Ibn Jurayj interprets the burden as transformation into apes and pigs.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r21] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مكحول | reports | Makhul and Salam ibn Sabur understand the unbearable burden as overpowering sexual desire; al-Naqqash also transmits this from Mujahid, Ata, and Makhul.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r22] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو الدرداء | reports | Abu al-Darda used to pray for refuge from sexual desire that could not be restrained.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r23] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · النخعي | reports | Al-Nakhaʿi interprets the unbearable burden as love.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r24] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · محمد بن عبد الوهاب | reports | Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab glosses the burden as passionate infatuation.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r25] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another explanation is severance of kinship ties.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r26] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another explanation is the gloating of enemies.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | God commands believers to ask not to be punished for sins committed in forgetfulness or error; this command supports that He grants what they request.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi, Ibn Jurayj, al-Rabiʿ, and Ibn Zayd explain isr as a solemn covenant and pledge.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd also explains isr as a sin for which there is neither expiation nor repentance.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مالك | reports | Malik glosses isr as a severe, difficult command.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · عطاء | reports | Ata explains isr as transformation into apes and pigs.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ثعلب | reports | Thalab transmits the gloss that isr means sin.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p764/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another gloss takes isr to mean an obligation w

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p765/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · وهب | reports | Wahb reports that Job was asked what was hardest in his affliction and answered: the enemies’ gloating.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p765/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddi identifies the burden imposed on earlier people as Israel’s restrictive prohibitions and heavy restraints.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p765/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Other explanations of the burden are hellfire or the whispers of the soul.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p765/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | These explanations are examples, not restrictions on the general meaning of the request.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p765/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The request for anything beyond capacity is broader than the earlier request for a burden like that imposed on predecessors; the intensified verb also underscores the request.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p765/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Abu reads the verb in an intensive form, comparable to the difference between جرح and جرّح.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p765/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Another interpretation distinguishes a first request to be spared difficult duties from a second request to be spared punishments inflicted on earlier communities for failing to keep them.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p765/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Ṭāqa is an anomalous verbal noun, not a productive pattern; it can mean absolute inability or a burden that is possible but severely difficult, mapping respectively to punishment or duties.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p765/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن الأنباري | reports | Ibn al-Anbari explains the plea as asking not to bear a load that is heavy to discharge even if one could endure it, like saying one cannot bear to look at someone one dislikes. | mentions 11:20
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p766/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Pardon removes punishment; forgiveness conceals the sin and protects from humiliation; mercy bestows beneficence, with each petition increasing in scope and intensity.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p766/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الراغب | reports | Al-Raghib similarly defines pardon as removing sin’s punishment, forgiveness as covering it and replacing it with kindness, and mercy as an outpouring of beneficence.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p766/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Specific readings assign pardon to protection from metamorphosis or actions, forgiveness to sinking or speech, mercy to the weighing of deeds, or each plea to death, the grave, and Judgment; Abu Hayyan says these restrictions lack evidence.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p766/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Mawla derives from waliya and can function as a verbal, temporal, or locative noun; in the sense of ruler, master, helper, or kinsman it is a lexicalized noun.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p766/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The ف in فانصرنا signals causation: because God is their master and manager, they ask Him to help them against enemies and instill courage while weakening the enemy.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p766/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The closing passage uses antithesis, semantic contrast, repetition, paronomasia, and ellipsis for rhetorical effect.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#2/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Lahā mā kasabat is an independent explanatory sentence: being answerable only for one's own deeds illustrates that God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#2/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Some distinguish the verbs: kasaba can mean earning for oneself or another, whereas iktasaba is narrower; Arabic says “he earns for his family” but not “he acquires his family,” and al-Ḥuṭayʾa's line uses kāsib.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#2/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī says evil takes the intensive iktasaba because the desirous self exerts effort to reach it, while good is described by the unmarked kasaba because it follows the path.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#2/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn ʿAṭiyya first suggests the different forms simply vary the wording elegantly, as in 86:17; the author instead sees a semantic distinction in the effort involved in good and evil. | mentions 86:17
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#2/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | The author prefers a distinction: good is earned without strain along God's prescribed way, while sin requires the intensified effort of breaking His prohibition.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#2/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Others find no difference, noting that the Qurʾān uses both forms for evil: 74:38, 6:164, and 33:58. | mentions 74:38, 6:164, 33:58
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#2/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abū al-Baqāʾ reports both the view that the forms are synonymous and the view that iftaʿala signals effort, making sin weighty in its consequences.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#2/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الواحدي | reports | Al-Wāḥidī says the sound linguistic view treats kasb and iktisāb as equivalent, citing Dhū al-Rummah's line that uses both forms together.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#3/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Tuʾākhidhnā is read with hamza from taking someone to task; the wāw reading either eases hamza to wāw by regular phonology or derives from wākhadhahu, as Abū al-Baqāʾ says.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#3/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The reciprocal form is used for one action because the sinner exposes himself to punishment by his deed, as if helping the punisher act against him; it may also be a conventional reciprocal such as sāfartu.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#3/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبي | reports | Ubayy reads rabbanā wa-lā tuḥammil ʿalaynā iṣran with a doubled mīm; al-Zamakhsharī explains this as intensifying “lay a burden upon.”
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#3/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī distinguishes the two doubled forms: the first intensifies carrying upon someone, while the second causatively shifts ḥamala from one object to two.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#3/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · النابغة | reports | Iṣr fundamentally means weight or severity; al-Nābigha's verse calls it a burden borne after the people have been exhausted.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#3/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Because a covenant is heavy, iṣr also means covenant or compact, as in God's covenant taken from the prophets in 3:81. | mentions 3:81
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#3/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The lām in lahā conveys ownership and the pleasure of good; ʿalā in ʿalayhā conveys evil's burden weighing upon its bearer.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#3/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | One view says even a slight good is credited graciously by God, while punishment follows only deliberate striving; the author says this depends on distinguishing the verb forms and finds that distinction strongest.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#4/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Iṣr in 7:157 means burdensome legal duties; it broadens to anything heavy, and some reportedly interpret it here as enemies' gloating, citing an unnamed poet. | mentions 7:157
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#4/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الحطيئة | reports | Iṣr can also mean affection or kinship; al-Ḥuṭayʾa says that no tie of kinship draws him to the person.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#4/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Iṣr may be the thing by which objects are bound; iṣār is the cord securing loads, from the verb aṣara, “to bind.”
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#4/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The noun iṣr is also transmitted with ḍamma on its hamza in a rare reading.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#4/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبي | reports | Ubayy's doubled mīm in lā tuḥammil ʿalaynā intensifies the action.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#4/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ṭāqa means ability and is an irregularly shortened verbal noun of aṭāqa; the expected form is iṭāqa, like other exceptional maṣdars such as ghāra, jāba, and nabāt, and it is not productive.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#4/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The author supports the exceptional verbal-noun pattern with Qurʾān 71:17 and a poetic example of ʿaṭāʾ. | mentions 71:17
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#5/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Mawlā is a mafʿal from wali/yali; here it is a verbal noun used for an agent, possibly with an omitted “possessor of our guardianship,” and it may also denote place or time.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#5/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The fāʾ marks causation: because God is their protector and manages their affairs, they ask Him to grant victory over their enemies.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#5/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The author illustrates this causal appeal with “You are generous, so grant me” and “You are a hero, so protect your sanctuary.”
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286#5/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The sūra contains many branches of learning; most have already been indicated, and an intelligent reader can infer what is suggested without explicit detail.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Wusʿahā is the second object of yukallifu. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says another object is omitted, but the Shaykh says that is true only at the verb's underlying valency, not in the surface syntax.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الشيخ | rejects | The Shaykh rejects an omitted object in the grammatical parse: wusʿahā itself is the second object, like dirhaman after an exceptive in “I gave Zayd only a dirham.”
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Wusʿ is what a person can contain or bear without constriction or exceeding capacity.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن أبي عبلة | reports | Ibn Abī ʿAblah reads the phrase as the past verb wasiʿahā; one parse supplies a deleted relative mā, making it the second object, a construction Basrans reject and Kufans allow, though the omission is weak.

:286/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن عطية | reports | Another parse of Ibn Abī ʿAblah's reading deletes the second object for clarity and makes the clause an adjective of it; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the reading permissible through inversion, comparing 2:255 and 20:98. | mentions 2:255, 20:98
[SAMIN-DURR:2:286/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | The sentence has no syntactic position, since it gives information; another analysis makes it an accusative supplement to “we hear and obey,” meaning they also said this.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p733#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · أبو مسعود | reports | The Prophet says that whoever recites the two closing verses of al-Baqara at night will find them sufficient; Ibn Kathir cites several transmission routes and gives no grading here.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p733#2/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · أبو ذر | reports | Abu Dharr reports the Prophet saying that he received the closing verses of al-Baqara from a treasure beneath the Throne, a gift given to no prophet before him.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p733#2/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · عبد الله | reports | Ibn Masud reports that during the Night Journey, at the Sidrat al-Muntaha in the sixth heaven, the Prophet received the five prayers, the closing verses of al-Baqara, and forgiveness for non-polytheists from his community even for grave sins. | mentions 53:16
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p734/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · عقبة بن عامر الجهني | reports | The Prophet tells Uqba ibn Amir to recite the final two verses of al-Baqara, saying they were given from beneath the Throne; Ibn Kathir calls the chain hasan, though the major collections do not include it.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p734/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · حذيفة | reports | Hudhayfa reports the Prophet saying that his community was favored with these verses from a treasure beneath the Throne, given to no one before or after him.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p734/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · علي | reports | Ali says that no person who understands Islam should go to sleep without reciting the closing verses, a treasure granted to the Prophet from beneath the Throne.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p734/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · علي | reports | In another transmission Ali adds Ayat al-Kursi to the nightly recitation of the closing verses, describing both as a treasure beneath the Throne. | mentions 2:255
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p734/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · النعمان بن بشير | reports | The Prophet says God wrote a book two thousand years before creating the heavens and earth, sent down from it the two verses ending al-Baqara, and that a house where they are recited is not approached by Satan for three nights. Al-Tirmidhi calls the report gharīb; al-Hakim calls it sahih by Muslim's standard, though they did not include it.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p735/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas reports that the Prophet laughed when reciting the closing verses and Ayat al-Kursi, saying they are from the Merciful's treasure beneath the Throne; reciting 4:123 and 53:39–41 instead made him grieve and submit. | mentions 2:255, 4:123, 53:39, 53:40, 53:41
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p735/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · معقل بن يسار | reports | The Prophet says he was given the Opening of the Book and the closing verses of al-Baqara from beneath the Throne, while the Mufassal was given as an extra voluntary portion.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p735/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas reports that Gabriel brought news of two lights never given to an earlier prophet: al-Fatiha and the closing verses of al-Baqara; every letter recited from them brings a gift.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p735/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · رجل | reports | In a report in al-Darimi, the Prophet names Ayat al-Kursi as the greatest verse and says he would choose the end of al-Baqara for his community because it contains every good of this world and the next. | mentions 2:255
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p736#2/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · جابر | reports | Jabir reports that after this verse was revealed, Gabriel told the Prophet that God had praised him and his community and invited him to ask; the Prophet then asked for the closing supplication beginning, 'God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity.'
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p737/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | God never imposes on a person more than they can bear; this expresses His kindness, mercy, and beneficence toward creation.

[ITQAN:v1p229#2/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · ابن الجزري | reports | Ibn al-Jazari says a reader should seek the fullest meaning and soundest pause, not adopt strained stopping or starting to force an interpretation; he gives several such examples, including splitting the final prayer into a vocative. | mentions 4:62, 31:13, 81:29, 2:158

[ITQAN:v2p500/r4] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | The coordinating and answer uses of lā do not occur in the Qur’an.

[SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p50#2/r3] SUYUTI-LUBAB, d. 911 · ابن عباس | reports | Muslim and others transmit from Ibn Abbas an account similar to Abu Hurayra’s report about the revelation of these closing verses. | mentions 2:284
[BURSEVI:v1p365#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The opening clause is God's own statement, not part of the believers' prayer.
[BURSEVI:v1p365#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | After 2:284 alarmed the Companions, they knelt before the Prophet, fearing they could not bear accounting for inner thoughts. [BURSEVI:v1p365#2/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Taklīf imposes a burden; wusʿ is what a person can accommodate without hardship. God, through favor and mercy to this community, assigns only what fits their capacity, as in 2:185. | mentions 2:185
[BURSEVI:v1p365#2/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | This shows that God has not actually imposed an impossible burden, not that such imposition is intrinsically impossible: its occurrence would make God's statement false, while an unrestricted negation does not establish impossibility.
[BURSEVI:v1p365#2/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The soul alone receives the reward for all the good it has earned and bears the punishment for all the evil it has acquired; no one else independently shares either account.
[BURSEVI:v1p365#2/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The verse uses the more effortful form اكتسبت for evil because the desired act involves striving, unlike good; the iftiʿāl form conveys exertion.

 The request implies that accountability for forgetfulness and error is possible because avoiding them is possible in some measure; otherwise the prayer would be meaningless.
[BURSEVI:v1p366/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet says this community is exempted from liability for error, forgetfulness, and coercion; earlier communities were liable for the first two.
[BURSEVI:v1p366/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Iṣr denotes a heavy load that pins its bearer in place, and here means burdensome religious duties.
[BURSEVI:v1p366/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Israelites faced severe duties: self-killing in repentance, cutting mistaken limbs and impurity, fifty daily prayers, mosque-only prayer, fasting restrictions, forbidden good things, quarter-wealth alms, and written records of nightly sins. | mentions 7:157
[BURSEVI:v1p366/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | God spared this community comparable strictures and earlier peoples' punishments; the Prophet describes his mission as the easy, tolerant upright way and says his community is spared sinking, metamorphosis, and drowning. | mentions 7:157
[BURSEVI:v1p366/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | This asks deliverance from unbearable punishments, after asking to avoid the onerous duties whose neglect could bring them; punishment is described as a load because those duties lead to it.
[BURSEVI:v1p367#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report says two verses from Paradise's treasures were written by the Merciful's hand two thousand years before creation, and reciting them after the final evening prayer suffices for night vigil.
[BURSEVI:v1p367#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet says whoever recites the final two verses of al-Baqara will be sufficed, either for night prayer or for the reckoning on Judgment Day.
[BURSEVI:v1p367#2/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Bursevi uses the Prophet's designation of al-Baqara as the Quran's tent to refute disapproval of calling it Surat al-Baqara.
[BURSEVI:v1p367#2/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet urges learning al-Baqara as a blessing, says abandoning it brings regret and sorcerers cannot master it, and the report links a house without its recitation for three nights with Satan's approach.
[BURSEVI:v1p367#2/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · معاذ | reports | Muʿādh used to say amen whenever he completed Surat al-Baqara.
[BURSEVI:v1p367#2/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · أبو الأسلم الديلمي | reports | Al-Daylami reports Muʿādh's capture of a date-stealing jinn; the Prophet foretold its return, and on its second capture it claimed that reciting al-Baqara's ending keeps devils out of a house that night.
[BURSEVI:v1p367/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · التيسير | reports | The request means not to impose duties that are difficult to sustain continually; it does not ask for the literally impossible, which cannot occur.
[BURSEVI:v1p367/r10] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | During the Miʿrāj, the Prophet recited the believers' response to 2:285 and then asked the petitions of this verse; God answered that error, forgetfulness, and coercion were lifted and granted the remaining requests. | mentions 2:285
[BURSEVI:v1p367/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Pardon means removing the traces of sins; forgiveness means concealing faults so the believer is not exposed before people.
[BURSEVI:v1p367/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · التيسير | reports | The two requests are not repetitive: pardon leaves the person unpunished and erases the sin, while forgiveness hides it from view; one may pardon while still mentioning and exposing a deed.
[BURSEVI:v1p367/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Believers ask both that God overlook their sins and conceal them, so their state is not publicly exposed.
[BURSEVI:v1p367/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Pardon and forgiveness precede the request for mercy because clearing away faults comes before adorning the servant with favor.
[BURSEVI:v1p367/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Mawlānā can mean our master while we are His servants, our helper, or the one who manages our affairs.
[BURSEVI:v1p367/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The plea asks God to help against disbelievers and repel their harm, as a guardian should defend those in his care; victory may come through conquest, argument, or defense.
[BURSEVI:v1p367/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The request for victory also seeks protection from devils, since they belong among the disbelieving enemies.
[BURSEVI:v1p367/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | In the Miʿrāj report, at the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary in the sixth heaven, the Prophet received the five prayers, the closing verses of al-Baqara, and forgiveness for any follower who avoids associating partners with God. | mentions 53:16
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p69#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | This is a fresh divine statement after believers accept the commands, revealing the grace and mercy built into the obligations before they ask for it.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p69#2/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The pronoun in lahā refers to the generic soul; reward and punishment are understood by ellipsis, with good implied by the beneficial lām.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p69#2/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The second mā denotes evil through the harmful ʿalā; iktasabat adds a sense of exertion because souls are drawn more intensely to acquiring evil.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p69#2/r12] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The unaugmented kasabat suits good, which does not involve the same striving; iktasabat signals the soul's inclination to work at evil.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p69#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Taklīf is imposing something burdensome; wusʿ is what human capacity can contain, or what is easy within capacity and below its limit.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p69#2/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | God's practice is to impose only what a person can bear, indeed sometimes less: five daily prayers despite capacity for more, and Ramadan despite capacity for additional fasting.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p69#2/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | This easing is grace, mercy, or special favor upon this community.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p69#2/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن أبي عبلة | reports | Ibn Abi ʿAblah recites wusʿahā with fatḥa on the sīn.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p69#2/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | On either gloss of wusʿ, the verse shows that impossible burdens do not actually occur, but it does not prove that such imposition is logically impossible.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p69#2/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | An objection says the easier-than-capacity gloss concerns this community alone and so cannot establish a universal rule against impossible burdens; Al-Alusi says the verse in any case does not prove their impossibility.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p69#2/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · مفتي الديار الرومية | reports | The fresh statement encourages observance and warns against neglect: each person's benefit from obedience and harm from disobedience return to that person, not to God.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p69#2/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | An alternative makes both clauses part of believers' separate utterances, praising them for gratitude that duties fit their capacity and that good benefits them while evil harms them, not God; Al-Alusi calls this remote in one respect and close in another.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | This asks relief from punishments that cannot be borne and that follow from prior burdens; describing punishment as loading is figurative, based on its consequences.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70#2/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو حيان | reports | Abu Hayyan explains the sequence: pardon answers the plea not to punish for error, forgiveness the plea not to impose burdens, and mercy the plea not to impose the unbearable; hence no repeated rabbana.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70#2/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Mawlānā means our owner and master, or the one who manages our affairs; it is a verbal noun used for an agent.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70#2/r12] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | When mawlā and sayyid are both used, Arabic usage puts mawlā first; al-Khansāʾ's verse is cited as evidence, though Al-Alusi has reservations about the criticism of the reverse order.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70#2/r13] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The clause may be understood as an instruction to say: You are our patron.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70#2/r14] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The requested victory is against enemy combatants or, more broadly, all unbelievers.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70#2/r15] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The fāʾ signals causation: because God is their patron and manager, they ask Him to grant victory, like asking generosity from a generous person.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Another view makes the request broader than the preceding one: the burden is pictured as impossible to bear for emphasis.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70#2/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | A further view treats this as asking to avoid literally impossible obligations and argues that the request proves such obligations are possible; Al-Alusi judges the argument weak.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70#2/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The doubled form here serves only to make the verb take a second object, not to intensify or multiply the action.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70#2/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | To pardon is to erase the traces of sins by withholding punishment.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70#2/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | To forgive is to conceal what is ugly and disclose what is beautiful.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70#2/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Mercy is gracious concern for the servants that brings increase.

I-FULL:v3p70#2/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | An alternative assigns pardon to deeds, forgiveness to words, and mercy to the weighing of the scales.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70#2/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Another alternative places pardon at death, forgiveness in the darkness of graves, and mercy amid the terrors of resurrection.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The passage resumes the believers' supplications after explaining the wisdom of obligation; it may also complete the narration of their utterances.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Iṣr is a weighty burden that confines its bearer; here it means difficult obligations.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Another interpretation takes iṣr as a sin for which there is no repentance, so the supplication asks protection from committing it.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70/r12] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Aṣāran is also read in the plural, and one reading doubles the tāʾ in tuḥammil.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70/r13] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The comparison is either an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning a burden like the one imposed earlier, or an adjective of iṣr itself.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70/r14] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Examples of Israelite burdens include killing oneself in repentance or retaliation, cutting impurity from clothing (some say the body), and giving a quarter of wealth as alms.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الحسن | reports | As transmitted by Abu Hayyan from al-Hasan, the phrase is an implied command to say this in prayer: God teaches servants how to ask so He may grant and reward them.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Muʾākhadha means punishment; the form fāʿala can carry the simple sense of fāʿala/afaʿala rather than reciprocal action.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | An alternative takes the reciprocal form literally: God holds the sinner accountable while the sinner, having no rescuer but God, appeals to Him as though demanding release; Al-Alusi calls this unsound without strained interpretation.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | One view takes forgetting as abandoning obligations and error as committing prohibitions, even deliberately, since sins are errors opposed to correctness.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | A second view means the prior negligence and inattention that usually cause forgetting or mistakes, and asks pardon for that antecedent shortcoming.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | A third view means actual forgetfulness and error: they could rationally bring punishment, like poison can kill when taken inadvertently, but God promised to overlook them as grace.
[ALUSI-FULL:v3p70/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الطبراني | reports | Al-Tabarani transmits a hadith that al-Nawawi grades ḥasan: the Prophet says his community is exempted for error, forgetfulness, and coercion.

 what one acquires could include a forgotten duty or unintended prohibited act.
[ELMALILI:2:286#2/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | A second construal says properly directed effort earns benefit, while blind striving after harm costs the person; capacity-calibrated divine duties guide people toward benefit and away from loss.

[ELMALILI:2:286#2/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | prefers | Most exegetes favor the first construal and attach the others to it; Elmalılı calls that first reading the main explanation because it is clear and contains the secrets of divine obligation.

[ELMALILI:2:286#3/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The petition remains necessary because wusʿ, though broader than capacity, is also commonly used for capacity; a burden proportionate to capacity may still be severe, so the prayer asks God to make the apparent sense one of ease.

[ELMALILI:2:286#3/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Someone who notices impurity on clothing but delays removing it and later forgets before praying is not excused, because the initial delay was negligent; someone who never noticed it is excused.

[ELMALILI:2:286#3/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Involuntary error does not change the intrinsic harm or unlawfulness of the resulting act, just as swallowed poison remains harmful or an accidental fall into a well remains dangerous; people must avoid such outcomes as far as possible.

[ELMALILI:2:286#3/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · رسول الله | reports | Elmalılı relates the plea to the Prophetic hadith, “My community’s error and forgetfulness are lifted,” while preserving liability for harm to others.
[ELMALILI:2:286#3/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Isr is a heavy burden or bond that holds the bearer in place, associated with captivity and confinement; it can also refer to a weighty covenant, subjection, the womb, and kinship.

[ELMALILI:2:286#4/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The plea covers unbearable burdens whether legal, which may drive people to revolt, or existential, which become torment and destruction; God could impose such things as a test or punishment, so believers ask for protection in every form.
